title: Urban Foxes and the Rise of City Wildlife
instructions: For questions 1-8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.
passage:
Walk through almost any British city after dark and there is a fair chance you will (1)___ a fox trotting along a pavement, seemingly unbothered by the traffic and streetlights around it. Foxes have, over the past half-century, (2)___ from a largely rural animal into one far more at home scavenging bins than hunting hedgerows.

Ecologists (3)___ this adaptability largely to the fox's famously varied diet: an animal willing to eat earthworms, discarded takeaways and garden birds with equal (4)___ is never going to starve in a city full of unsecured bins.

This lack of fussiness has not endeared foxes to everyone. Gardeners accuse them of (5)___ up flowerbeds in search of grubs, while some parents worry, probably unnecessarily, about a fox (6)___ too close to young children.

Councils have largely (7)___ down calls for mass culls, pointing out that removing foxes from an area rarely works for long: new animals simply (8)___ the vacated territory within weeks.

questions.explanation: 'Spot' means to notice or catch sight of something briefly, fitting a chance nighttime sighting. 'Stare' needs 'at' and implies a sustained look; 'view' suggests formal, deliberate observation; 'watch' implies following something over time, not a fleeting glimpse.

'Morph from X into Y' is an established collocation for a gradual transformation. 'Altered' is normally transitive ('altered something'); 'varied from...to' means 'ranged between', not 'changed into'; 'shifted' typically pairs with 'to', not 'into'.

'Attribute X to Y' means to say Y is the cause of X. 'Accredit' means to officially certify; 'contribute to' means to help cause something, which would reverse the sentence's logic; 'distribute' means to share something out.

'With equal nonchalance' means showing the same casual indifference regardless of the food on offer. 'Arrogance' means excessive pride, 'diligence' means careful hard work, and 'reluctance' means unwillingness — the opposite of eating happily.

'Dig up' means to excavate soil in search of something, fitting grubs buried in a flowerbed. 'Pick up' means to lift; 'back up' means to support or reverse; 'make up' means to invent a story or reconcile after an argument.

'Stray too close to' means to move nearer than is safe, by accident. 'Lurk' means to hide and wait; 'drift' suggests slow, aimless movement; 'roam' implies covering a wide area rather than approaching one specific point.

'Turn down' means to reject a request or proposal. 'Put down' means to euthanise an animal or criticise someone; 'shut down' and 'close down' both mean to stop an operation running, not to refuse a request.

'Recolonise' is transitive, taking 'the vacated territory' directly as its object. 'Migrate' and 'relocate' are normally intransitive and would need 'to'; 'transfer' means to move something else from one place to another, not to settle into a place.
